slides.title: System Design Framework Overview
content: A system design framework is a structured approach to solving open-ended design problems
System design questions are intentionally vague and test thinking, not memorization
Without structure, designs become random and incomplete
Framework ensures clarity, scalability thinking, and proper communication
Interviewers evaluate reasoning, trade-offs, and structured problem solving

slides.title: Why Framework is Important
content: Helps avoid jumping directly into components without understanding requirements
Prevents missing important system constraints
Avoids over-engineering in early stages
Provides a clear step-by-step approach to design problems
Improves communication and confidence during interviews

slides.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements
content: Identify what the system should do through functional requirements
Understand system performance through non-functional requirements
Functional requirements include features like upload, search, and messaging
Non-functional requirements include scalability, availability, latency, consistency, and durability
Always ask about users, traffic, data size, and real-time needs before designing

slides.title: Step 2: Estimation
content: Perform rough calculations to estimate system scale and feasibility
Estimate daily active users, queries per second, storage, and bandwidth
Helps identify bottlenecks and system constraints early
Supports decisions like database choice and caching strategy
Focus on logical reasoning rather than exact numbers

slides.title: Step 3: High-Level Design
content: Design overall system architecture using major components
Include client, load balancer, servers, database, cache, CDN, and message queues
Start with simple block diagrams before going into details
Explain how data flows through the system step by step
Provides a clear big-picture understanding of the system

slides.title: Step 4: Deep Dive
content: Focus on one or two critical components for detailed explanation
Analyze database design, caching, sharding, replication, or consistency
Identify and solve performance bottlenecks
Explain design decisions with proper reasoning
Always justify why a component is chosen for deep analysis

slides.title: Trade-Off Analysis
content: System design always involves choosing between different trade-offs
SQL provides strong consistency but is harder to scale
NoSQL offers scalability and flexibility but weaker consistency
Strong consistency ensures accurate data but increases latency
Caching improves performance but may return stale data

slides.title: Handling Bottlenecks
content: A bottleneck is the slowest component limiting system performance
Common bottlenecks include database, network, CPU, and disk I/O
Use caching to reduce load on databases
Apply replication and sharding for scalability
Use load balancing and asynchronous processing to improve performance

slides.title: Communication Strategy
content: Think aloud while designing to show your reasoning
Clearly explain assumptions and decisions
Use simple diagrams for better understanding
Adapt your design based on interviewer feedback
Avoid silence, overengineering, and random explanations

slides.title: Time Management
content: Spend initial time clarifying requirements properly
Allocate time for estimation before designing
Focus most time on high-level design and deep dive
Reserve time for discussing scaling and improvements
Follow a structured timeline to cover all aspects efficiently

slides.title: Common Mistakes
content: Skipping requirement clarification step
Ignoring estimation and scale calculations
Jumping directly into detailed design
Not considering failure scenarios
Avoiding discussion of trade-offs

slides.title: What Interviewers Evaluate
content: Ability to handle ambiguity in open-ended problems
Understanding of system scalability and distributed systems
Capability to analyze trade-offs and make decisions
Clarity in communication and structured thinking
Focus on reasoning rather than memorized answers or exact numbers
